lead: Retinyl esters are fatty-acid esters of retinol (vitamin A), the main form in which the body stores vitamin A, chiefly as retinyl palmitate in the liver [1][2]. In cosmetics, retinyl palmitate, acetate and propionate are used as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and tretinoin [3].

In skin, esters are described as converting to retinol and then to retinoic acid, though Wikipedia states neither absorption nor conversion is very efficient [3]. No trials of retinyl esters for cosmetic appearance were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: Dietary retinoids are needed for growth, vision, immune function, reproduction and skin barrier function, and the body must obtain them from food [2]. Retinol is esterified by LRAT for storage and released by retinyl ester hydrolases; hormone-sensitive lipase can hydrolyze retinyl esters [1][3]. Retinyl esters also act as substrates in the visual cycle, where RPE65 converts them toward 11-cis-retinal [4][3].

No studies found of retinyl esters used on skin for appearance. Related work covers vitamin A status and absorption, for example a registered trial of vitamin A absorption from fortified bouillon [5].

Preformed vitamin A in excess can cause hypervitaminosis A [3]. Retinyl palmitate in sunscreens drew public debate after animal studies in which topical retinyl palmitate or retinoic acid increased tumor rates in UV-exposed mice. A 2010 toxicological analysis reported no convincing evidence that retinyl palmitate is carcinogenic in sunscreens, while a later National Toxicology Program report on SKH-1 mice found worsened tumor rates [3].
